subject: 건반 악기가 바뀐 순간
title: When the keyboard learned to play loudly and softly
content: Earlier keyboard instruments plucked their strings with a quill, which produces a bright tone at a fixed volume regardless of how the key is struck. Replacing the pluck with a hammer that strikes and rebounds gave the player control over loudness through the fingers, and this single change reorganised the whole musical culture built around the instrument. The mechanism had to be invented rather than adapted. A hammer that stays against the string damps it, so it must be thrown and then fall back, and the escapement that permits this while still allowing rapid repetition took decades of refinement by several makers. Early examples were criticised for being harder to play than what they replaced. Composers responded slowly and then completely. Music written for the older instrument uses ornament and rhythmic activity to sustain interest across notes that cannot swell, while music for the new one uses a long line that grows and recedes, and a whole vocabulary of gradual change entered the notation because there was finally something to notate. The instrument kept growing. Iron frames permitted greater string tension, heavier hammers produced more sound, and the range extended in both directions, so a work written early in the tradition is played on an instrument its composer never heard. This is a standing problem for performance. Something was lost as well. The older instrument's clarity in dense counterpoint has never been matched by its successor, whose sustained tone blurs interweaving lines, which is why performers of certain repertoire returned to the earlier instrument in the twentieth century and found audiences who preferred it.

subject: 푸가의 규칙
title: A form built from one idea pursued
content: A fugue takes a short melodic subject and develops it by having voices enter in succession, each stating the subject while the others continue, so the texture accumulates without any voice dropping into accompaniment. It is among the strictest musical forms and it is not a fixed template. The opening establishes the material. One voice states the subject alone, a second answers it at a fixed interval while the first continues with a counter-subject, and further voices enter in turn until all are present. This exposition is the one part of the form that convention governs closely, and everything after it varies. What follows is a series of statements separated by passages built from fragments of the material. Those passages modulate, so each return of the subject arrives in a different key, and the composer decides how many returns there are and where. A fugue can therefore be short or enormous, and nothing about the form determines its length. The devices are technical and audible. A subject can be inverted, stretched to twice its length, compressed, or overlapped with itself so that a second entry begins before the first has finished. Listeners who know the subject hear these operations as events, which is why the form rewards familiarity with the material more than almost any other. Its difficulty is real and it is not the point. Writing a fugue that obeys the rules is an exercise; writing one whose subject is worth pursuing and whose returns arrive where the music needs them is composition, and the tradition distinguishes sharply between the two.

subject: 왈츠가 퍼진 경로
title: A dance that scandalised and then conquered
content: A couple dance in triple time, with the partners holding each other and turning continuously, spread across Europe in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries and provoked objections that now read as extraordinary. The objections tell us what the dance actually changed. Earlier social dancing arranged couples in sets, with partners changing and the whole room forming a figure. The new dance took one pair, put them in a closed hold, and let them turn independently of everybody else, so the floor became a collection of private units rather than a single pattern. Contemporary complaints focused on exactly this. The hold was the specific scandal. Partners faced each other in continuous contact for the length of a piece, which no respectable dance had required, and published objections describe it in terms that leave no doubt about what was being objected to. Several courts banned it and the bans failed. Music followed the dance. Composers wrote for it in quantity, the form acquired an introduction and a coda and grew into concert music, and a family of composers in one city built an industry on it, which is an unusual case of a social dance generating a substantial art repertoire. Its structure explains the persistence. Turning continuously in triple time produces a physical sensation that dancers describe consistently across two centuries, and the dance requires little instruction, so it spread to any room with music. What began as an affront to how a ballroom should look became the standard against which later social dances were measured.

subject: 아악의 느린 박
title: Music so slow that the pulse must be counted
content: A tradition of Korean court music preserves tempos far slower than any other living musical practice. A single beat may last several seconds, a phrase may extend for a minute, and listeners unfamiliar with the tradition frequently cannot locate the pulse at all, which is a genuine difficulty rather than inattention. The slowness is historical rather than original. Comparison of surviving notation across centuries shows that the same pieces were performed considerably faster in earlier periods and decelerated steadily, so the current tempo is the endpoint of a long drift. Similar deceleration has been documented in other court traditions, and the reasons proposed include ceremonial dignity and the absence of any pressure toward brevity. Instruments shape the effect. Long sustained tones on wind instruments, a stone chime and a bronze bell marking structural points, and a zither whose notes decay slowly produce a texture in which individual events are separated by silence, so a listener attends to single sounds rather than to a line. Melody in the ordinary sense is difficult to follow. Ornament carries the expression. Each sustained tone is shaped — bent, swelled, or given a slow vibrato — and practitioners regard these inflections as the substance of the art, so two performances differing only in ornament are as different as two readings of a text. Its function was never entertainment. The music accompanied state ritual, its structure corresponded to the ceremony rather than to any listener's attention, and hearing it in a concert hall removes the frame it was built for, which is a difficulty that every surviving court tradition now faces. Transmission has been institutional rather than familial. Court musicians were trained in a state office, the repertoire was recorded in notation that specifies pitch and duration, and that documentation is why the tradition survived periods when the court that sponsored it did not. Popular traditions transmitted only by ear lost far more.

subject: 사군자라는 소재 체계
title: Four plants that a painter learns first
content: East Asian ink painting traditions build their first training around four plants — plum, orchid, chrysanthemum, and bamboo — each tied to a season and to a quality of character. A student paints these for years before trying anything else, and seeing why explains how the tradition passes on its method. Each plant asks for a different brush stroke. Bamboo asks for a firm downward press that gives a segment of even width; orchid leaves need a long curving stroke that thins and swells; plum branches need a dry brush pulled against the paper; chrysanthemum petals need many short checked marks. Together they cover most of the movements the tradition uses. The subjects are therefore exercises with meaning attached. Because each carries a symbolic association — endurance in cold, modesty, resilience, uprightness — a student practising a stroke is simultaneously absorbing the tradition's vocabulary of character, and the paintings they eventually give away carry those meanings to their recipients. Judgement is possible because the subject is fixed. A viewer who has seen a thousand bamboo paintings can judge a new one closely, since the subject offers nothing new and all of it rests on the handling, which is why the tradition uses these subjects to weigh painters across centuries. Amateurs and professionals both painted them. The subjects require no studio and little material, so scholars who painted as an accomplishment used them constantly, and a substantial portion of surviving ink painting consists of these four plants made by people whose main occupation was something else entirely. Teachers judge progress by the stroke rather than by the likeness. A student whose bamboo leaves are correctly shaped but drawn hesitantly has not advanced, while one whose leaves are irregular yet drawn with a single confident movement has, and this criterion is applied consistently across the four subjects. It also explains why the tradition values speed.

subject: 장수 상징의 도상
title: Pictures made to wish somebody a long life
content: A recurring set of motifs in East Asian decorative art — pine, crane, deer, turtle, rock, water, cloud, bamboo, and a particular fungus — appears together on screens, ceramics, textiles, and furniture. The grouping is not a landscape but a message, and objects carrying it were made as gifts for particular occasions. Each element carries an established association with endurance. Pine stays green through winter, cranes and turtles were believed to live extraordinarily long, rocks and mountains outlast everything, and the fungus was held to confer longevity. Assembling them produces an accumulation of the same wish rather than a scene, which is why the compositions look crowded to viewers who read them as pictures. The arrangement follows conventions rather than observation. Elements appear at scales that no viewpoint would produce, animals stand beside plants they would never encounter, and the whole is organised for balance and legibility. A viewer within the tradition reads the assembly as a list; one outside it sees an impossible landscape. Occasions determined the object. Such decoration was commissioned for birthdays of the elderly, for weddings, and for retirements, so the motif appears overwhelmingly on things given rather than bought for oneself, and the format follows the occasion — a screen for a household, a bowl for a table, embroidery for a garment. The motifs travelled across the region and across media. Their consistency over many centuries and several countries makes them useful to specialists, since the presence and treatment of particular elements dates an object and locates its origin more reliably than style alone.

subject: 낙관과 인장의 기능
title: The red marks on an ink painting
content: An East Asian painting frequently carries several red seal impressions, and they are not decoration. Each records a relationship to the work — who made it, who owned it, who admired it — so the accumulated marks are a document of the object's history stamped onto its surface. The painter's own seal comes first, usually beside a signature or an inscription. It may give a name, a studio name, or a phrase the painter used, and artists commonly owned several, so the particular seal used can date a work within the artist's career. Forgers have always attended to seals, and their study is a specialised field. Collectors added their own. Owning a work entitled a collector to impress a seal, and a painting that passed through many hands accumulates them, sometimes in considerable numbers. Where a famous collector's seal appears, the object's value rises, since the mark is evidence of a history that can be traced. Emperors who collected extensively left seals that specialists recognise immediately. Placement is governed by courtesy. Seals should not obscure the image, and a collector adding one to a crowded work must find space that earlier owners left, so the arrangement records an order of precedence. Careless placement was criticised, and a few historical figures were notorious for stamping too large and too often. The seals are carved objects in their own right. Cutting a seal in stone is a distinct art with its own masters, its own styles of script, and its own connoisseurship, so a painting may carry impressions made by several seal carvers, each of whom is identifiable to a specialist.

subject: 족자와 계절 교체
title: Pictures that are hung for a season and put away
content: In traditions using hanging scrolls, a household does not display its paintings permanently. A single work is hung in an alcove, kept for a period, and then rolled and stored while another takes its place, so the room shows one picture at a time and the choice changes with the season or the occasion. Preservation is one reason. Ink and pigment on paper or silk fade under light, and a work displayed continuously deteriorates within a generation, while one shown for a few weeks a year survives for centuries. The rotation is therefore a conservation practice that a culture built into ordinary domestic life. The aesthetic follows from it. A single work receives the attention that a wall of pictures divides, the alcove is designed to frame it, and the flowers and objects placed nearby are chosen to accompany that particular scroll. Changing the scroll changes the room's whole arrangement. Selection carries meaning. A work depicting a plum branch is hung when plum blossoms, a snowy landscape in winter, and a subject appropriate to a guest's circumstances when a guest is expected, so the choice is a statement made to whoever enters. Visitors were expected to notice. Storage is part of the object. A scroll is rolled around a rod, wrapped in cloth, and placed in a fitted wooden box, which is frequently inscribed with the work's title and provenance, so the box accumulates documentation. Specialists read those boxes as evidence, and a work separated from its box has lost part of its record.

subject: 대나무 공예의 구조
title: Working a material that is hollow and split
content: Bamboo is neither wood nor grass in its working properties. It is hollow, its fibres run only along its length, and it splits with almost no effort in that direction while resisting cutting across, so every craft tradition using it works with the split rather than against it. Splitting is the fundamental operation. A knife started at one end travels the whole length with a push, producing strips of even width, and a maker judges thickness by feel while splitting rather than by measuring afterwards. Repeated splitting produces strips fine enough to weave, and the finest work uses material that is nearly thread. The outer skin behaves differently from the inner layers. The surface is dense, glossy, and water resistant, while the interior is soft and absorbent, so a maker chooses which side faces outward according to whether the object must repel water or take a finish, and strips are frequently split to separate the two. Heat makes it bend. Bamboo held over flame becomes pliable and holds its new shape on cooling, which permits curves that no amount of force would achieve cold, and traditions producing furniture and tools rely on this entirely. The technique requires judging the moment before scorching. Age and season govern the harvest. Culms cut in the wrong season carry more starch and are eaten by insects within a year, and material that is too young lacks strength while too old becomes brittle, so gathering is done at a particular time and the material is stored for a period before use. Makers describe this preparation as most of the craft.

subject: 백자의 절제
title: A ceramic that shows nothing but its shape
content: White porcelain with little or no decoration became the dominant ware in Korea for several centuries, and the preference was ideological before it was aesthetic. A ruling class committed to restraint regarded elaborate ornament as improper, and the pottery it commissioned expressed that position. The material is demanding precisely because it hides nothing. Any irregularity in the body, any unevenness in the glaze, and any distortion in firing is visible on an undecorated white surface, so a form that would pass with a pattern over it fails without one. Potters working in this tradition had to achieve a purity of body and an evenness of glaze that decorated wares do not require. The forms carry the whole expression. Proportion, the swell of a shoulder, the turn of a rim, and the relation between a body and a foot are what a viewer attends to, and the tradition developed a critical vocabulary for exactly these, so pieces are compared on qualities that photographs convey poorly. The whiteness is not uniform. Different clay bodies and glaze recipes produce warm, blue-tinged, and grey-tinged whites, and the tradition distinguished them and associated each with particular periods and kilns, so what looks like one colour to an outsider is a range to a specialist. Where decoration appears it is sparse. A single motif in underglaze blue or iron brown on an otherwise empty surface makes the emptiness legible, and the placement of that motif — high on a shoulder, low near a foot — is the whole composition. Later collectors from other traditions valued exactly this restraint, which had originated as a moral position rather than a taste.

subject: 온돌이 정한 좌식 생활
title: A heated floor and everything that follows from it
content: A traditional Korean house is heated from below. Flues run beneath the floor from a firebox at one end to a chimney at the other, the stone and clay above them absorb heat and release it slowly, and the warm surface is the floor people sit and sleep on. Almost everything about how such a house is inhabited follows from that arrangement. Furniture accordingly stays low or disappears entirely. Since the warmest surface is the floor, sitting on it is comfortable rather than a hardship, so chairs become unnecessary and tables are constructed at a height suited to somebody seated on the ground. Storage moves to chests and to shelves, and bedding is rolled away in the morning, which lets one room serve several purposes across a day. Room dimensions are constrained by the system. Heat weakens as it travels from the firebox, so a room larger than the flues can serve will be warm at one end and cold at the other, and traditional plans accordingly use several small rooms rather than a few large ones. The arrangement of such a house is therefore partly a diagram of its heating. The kitchen supplies the heat. A firebox for cooking sits below floor level at one end of the heated room, so the same fuel warms the floor and prepares the meal, and the kitchen floor is therefore lower than the rooms beside it. This connection between cooking and heating governed the daily rhythm, since the floor was warmest immediately after meals. Modern versions circulate hot water through pipes rather than smoke through flues. The heat source changed completely while the resulting habits did not, so contemporary apartments in the same tradition are still constructed around a warm floor and the low furniture appropriate to it.

subject: 서원의 배치 원리
title: A school arranged so that study faces memory
content: Private academies established in Korea from the sixteenth century combined two functions in one complex: teaching the living and honouring a scholar of the past. The plan expresses that combination, and reading it explains what such institutions understood themselves to be doing. The site is chosen away from towns. Locations near mountains and streams were preferred, on the reasoning that study requires quiet and that landscape supports contemplation, so the approach is frequently a walk from the nearest settlement. This was a statement about what learning required. The plan divides into two zones along an axis. The lecture hall and the students' quarters occupy the front, and the shrine holding the memorial tablets stands at the rear on higher ground, so the everyday work of study sits below and before the object of reverence. A visitor moves from the ordinary to the commemorative, and students lived with that arrangement daily. The lecture hall is open. A raised floor with removable partitions faces a courtyard, so teaching occurred in a space that could be closed in winter and opened in summer, and the master sat at the centre with students to either side rather than in rows. Dormitories face each other across the same courtyard, which put the whole community in view of itself. Libraries and printing sat alongside. Several such academies held substantial collections and cut their own woodblocks, so the institution produced texts as well as teaching them, and the surviving blocks are now studied as evidence for what each academy considered worth transmitting. The academies also served as centres of local influence. Their members corresponded with officials, took positions on questions of the day, and accumulated land and privileges, so a state that had encouraged their founding eventually moved against them. Several hundred were closed by decree in the nineteenth century, and the surviving examples are those that were spared as representative institutions.

subject: 목탑과 전탑의 구조
title: Towers built of timber and of brick
content: Buddhist pagodas in East Asia were built in wood, in brick, and in stone, and the choice of material determined the form far more than any regional taste. Comparing the timber and brick traditions shows how a single symbolic type adapts to what the material permits. Timber towers rise on a frame. Columns carry the load, bracket sets transfer it outward to support deep eaves, and each storey repeats the arrangement, so the structure is light for its height and flexible in an earthquake. The eaves can project far because the brackets carry them, which produces the characteristic profile of curving roofs at every level. Fire and rot are the enemies. Almost every early timber pagoda has burned at least once, and the surviving examples are those that escaped both war and lightning, so the tradition is documented far more by foundation stones than by standing buildings. Rebuilding was routine and each rebuilding altered proportions. Brick towers solve durability and lose the eaves. Masonry cannot cantilever, so brick pagodas imitate the timber form with shallow corbelled courses that suggest eaves without projecting far, and the resulting silhouette is steeper and plainer. They survive in numbers that the timber tradition does not. The interior differs completely. A timber tower has usable floors and stairs; a brick one is frequently solid or holds a narrow shaft, so it functions as a monument to be circled rather than a building to be entered. The same religious meaning is served by two structures that a visitor experiences in entirely different ways.

subject: 산대놀이의 무대
title: Playing on a temporary stage in the open
content: A tradition of Korean masked drama was performed on and around structures erected for the occasion — raised platforms, decorated frames, or simply cleared ground with the audience surrounding it. Because the stage was temporary, it shaped the form as decisively as any script would have. Nothing in such a play could depend on scenery. A play performed wherever a crowd could gather cannot rely on a painted backdrop or a fixed entrance, so location is established by speech and by movement, and a performer stating where they are supplies the setting. This is the same solution that outdoor traditions elsewhere reached independently. Its audience surrounds the action. Performers must be legible from every side, which excludes staging built around a single viewpoint and favours movement in the round, large gesture, and masks that read at a distance. Entrances happen through the crowd rather than from wings, so the boundary between watching and performing is thin. The occasion determined everything else. Such plays were performed at festivals, at markets, and for visiting officials, and the audience arrived for the occasion rather than for the play, so a performance competed with everything else happening and had to hold attention without any of the theatre's usual advantages. Musicians accompanied it throughout. A small ensemble played between and during scenes, marked entrances, and set the rhythm for dance sections, and the players sat at the edge of the performing area in full view, which is an arrangement that outdoor traditions generally adopt because there is nowhere to hide them. Costume compensated for the absence of scenery. Masks identified each figure immediately, garments indicated rank and occupation, and a performer changing masks became a different character in view of the audience, so the whole apparatus of identification was carried on the body. Nothing had to be built, which is exactly what a travelling company required.

subject: 유랑 연희패의 종목
title: What a travelling troupe could perform
content: Itinerant performing companies in Korea carried a repertoire of several distinct acts and presented them in sequence over an evening. The combination looks miscellaneous and it was carefully assembled, since a troupe travelling with limited people had to fill a whole occasion from whatever its members could do. The programme mixed kinds deliberately. Percussion music and dance, tightrope walking, acrobatics on the ground, masked drama, and puppet theatre appeared in a single evening, so an audience received music, spectacle, comedy, and narrative in turn. The variation held attention across hours in a way that any single form could not. Each act made different demands. The rope walker needed a rigged line and a level site; the puppet stage needed a screen and operators concealed behind it; the masked play needed open ground. A troupe therefore chose its site for what the whole programme required, and the order of acts followed what could be set up while something else was happening. Members were multiply skilled. A performer might drum in one act, take a role in another, and assist with the puppets in a third, since a company small enough to travel could not carry specialists, and training accordingly covered several disciplines. Their social position was low and their independence was real. Such troupes stood outside the settled order, which brought contempt and permitted a directness that settled performers could not risk, and the satirical content of the masked plays they carried is inseparable from the fact that the performers moved on the next day.

subject: 승무의 호흡
title: A dance built on breathing
content: A Korean solo dance performed in a robe with extremely long sleeves is organised around the breath. The dancer inhales as the arms rise, holds at the top of the movement, and releases as they descend, so the visible motion is a consequence of breathing rather than an accompaniment to it. The sleeves make the breath visible. Lengths of cloth extending well beyond the hands continue every gesture after the arm stops, so a movement that ends still produces a shape that travels outward and settles, and the timing of that settling depends entirely on how the arm was accelerated and stopped. A dancer controls cloth she is not touching. Weight shifts drive the lower body. The knees bend and straighten in a cycle that raises and lowers the whole figure, which the tradition describes in terms of drawing up and pressing down, and this vertical motion rather than any travel across the floor supplies the dance's pulse. A dancer may cover very little ground in a long passage. The drum section is the climax. Late in the dance the performer moves to a hanging drum and plays it, and the rhythmic complexity there contrasts with the sustained slowness of everything preceding, so the whole structure is a long accumulation released into activity. Its origins are disputed. The dance is associated with Buddhist practice and its costume resembles a monastic robe, and scholars differ over whether it descends from a religious dance or was assembled later from several sources, with the surviving evidence supporting both accounts partially.

subject: 궁중 정재의 형식
title: Dance performed for a seated ruler
content: Court dance in Korea was performed at banquets and ceremonies before an audience whose most important member sat still at one end of the hall, and because that seat never moved, the whole art was built around it. Every feature of this form follows from that arrangement, and setting it beside popular dance of the same period shows how completely the setting shapes the art. Its orientation is fixed. Dancers face the ruler's position, formations are symmetrical about the axis leading to it, and movements that would turn a performer's back are avoided or handled with prescribed transitions. Therefore a dance made for an audience on all sides could not be reused here without change. Its tempo is slow and its range of movement is small. Large or rapid motion would be improper in that presence, so expression works within a narrow band, and although the range is small, the tradition built a vocabulary of controlled gestures that a knowing viewer reads precisely. Dancers describe this restraint as the difficulty. Sung text is part of this performance too. Dancers sing verses at prescribed points, an introductory announcement states what will be performed, and the whole occasion is scripted, so the dance sits inside a ceremony rather than constituting one. Records specifying every element survive in considerable detail. Costume and the objects held carry rank. Their colours, headdresses, and objects are assigned by role and occasion rather than chosen, and the surviving manuals illustrate them exactly. This documentation is why the tradition could be reconstructed after periods of interruption, which popular forms transmitted only by practice could not. The repertoire was recorded in detail and this saved it. Illustrated manuals produced by the court specify formations, costumes, properties, and the verses to be sung, so pieces that fell out of performance could later be reconstructed from documents rather than from memory. Traditions without such records lost comparable repertoires entirely during the same period.

subject: 시조의 삼장 구조
title: A poem in three lines and a turn
content: A Korean poetic form consists of three lines with a prescribed syllable structure, and the third line begins with a group that breaks the established pattern. That break is the form's central device, and everything about how such poems work depends on it. The first two lines establish. They present a situation, an image, or a proposition in parallel construction, so a listener settles into a rhythm and expects it to continue, and the poet uses that expectation deliberately. Nothing in the first two lines announces what is coming. The third line opens with a syllable group of a different length. The disruption is small in count and large in effect, since the ear has been prepared for one shape and receives another, and the content placed there is conventionally a turn — a reversal, a question, an unexpected conclusion. The form and the sense change together. Its origins are oral. The poems were sung rather than read, with a melodic setting that stretched the syllables enormously, so what looks brief on a page occupied several minutes in performance, and the structure served singing before it served reading. Modern presentation as text loses that entirely. The form has survived across a long period of literary change. It was used by court officials, by professional entertainers, and by anonymous authors, and its brevity made it transmissible orally, so a considerable number of examples survive from populations that left no other written record. That range of authorship is unusual for a fixed poetic form.

subject: 한시의 압축
title: Poems written in a language nobody spoke
content: Poets across East Asia wrote in literary Chinese for many centuries, including in countries where that tongue was never spoken. The practice made huge bodies of verse in Korea, Japan, and Vietnam, and seeing what it asked of a poet explains features of those literatures that look odd on their own. Because the written tongue was shared while the sounds were not, something unusual followed. A poem made in one country was read by scholars in another, who took it in fully while sounding every character in their own way, so the tradition carried a literature that all could read and none could hear alike. Rhyme was determined by rhyme books rather than by any speaker's ear. Compression is the form's central discipline. Characters hold meaning tightly, small grammar words can be dropped, and a line of five or seven characters must hold a whole image, so poets built a manner of setting things side by side in which the links are left for the reader. Translation into any language with required grammar therefore adds what the original had left open. Allusion carries much of its sense as well. A poem's force frequently depends on recognising a phrase from an earlier work, and educated readers shared a corpus deep enough that a two character reference could invoke a whole situation. Although this makes such poems nearly opaque without notes today, it made them immediate for their own audience. This tradition ended when that education did. Once literary Chinese ceased to be taught as the language of learning, the ability to compose and to read fluently disappeared within a generation, leaving literatures that their own descendants require translation to approach. The practice also produced a shared community of readers. A scholar in one country could exchange written poems with a visitor from another without either speaking the other language, and diplomatic missions routinely included such exchanges, so the tradition functioned as an international literary culture conducted entirely on paper.

subject: 판소리계 소설의 성립
title: Novels written down from a sung tradition
content: Several Korean novels survive in many versions that differ widely, and that variation is explained by where they came from: they were taken down from a sung storytelling art rather than written as books. The tie between the sung form and the printed one is unusually well recorded. The performances varied by singer and by occasion. A singer built an evening from remembered scenes, drew out what a crowd took to, and cut what it did not, so no two tellings were alike and no version was the first. Written texts capture particular realisations of this. Transcription happened repeatedly and independently. Different scribes at different times set down different singers, and printers later made editions from these, so the texts that survive fall into families that scholars group by what they share. Some versions run to several times the length of others. The prose retains marks of singing. Passages that were sung keep a raised rhythmic manner with matched phrases, while the linking parts read as plain prose, so the turn taking of the performance survives on the page. A reader familiar with the tradition can identify which passages were which. Endings differ. Some versions resolve as the performance tradition did, others were altered by printers to suit a reading audience, and a few carry conclusions that reverse the moral of others, so the question of what a given story means depends on which text is consulted. Editors producing modern editions must choose, and their choices have shaped how the works are understood. Scholars have used the variation as evidence rather than treating it as corruption. Comparing versions reveals which episodes were stable and which were freely elaborated, which indicates what audiences responded to, and that information about performance would be unavailable if a single authorised text had survived instead.

subject: 야담집의 편집
title: Collections of stories somebody heard
content: A genre of Korean writing consists of short narratives collected by literate men from oral circulation — anecdotes about officials, accounts of strange occurrences, stories about ordinary people — assembled into books. The genre sits between literature and record, and its editing reveals what the collectors thought they were doing. The stories were gathered rather than composed. Compilers state that they heard a tale from a traveller, an official, or a servant, and the attribution is part of the text, so the reader is told where the material came from. This framing distinguishes the genre from fiction and it does not make the contents reliable. Selection reveals interests. Compilers favoured stories about the workings of office, about reversals of fortune, and about people of low standing who acted well, and the accumulation across a collection produces an implicit commentary on the society that the compiler never states directly. Reading a whole collection is different from reading its parts. The prose is plain. Written in literary Chinese or in mixed script, the style avoids the ornamentation that formal composition required, which the compilers occasionally apologise for, and that plainness is why the collections preserve turns of speech and detail that polished writing removes. Historians use them for exactly this. Their status was low and their survival was good. Regarded as minor writing, such collections were copied and circulated widely rather than preserved carefully, and the resulting abundance of manuscripts gives scholars something they lack for more prestigious genres: many versions of the same material, transmitted independently.

subject: 신문 연재만화의 칸
title: Telling a joke in four panels
content: Newspaper comic strips developed under constraints that no other narrative form faces. The space is fixed and small, the audience reads while doing something else, and the instalment must work alone while contributing to a series that may run for decades. The conventions that resulted are precise. Four panels became a standard because the structure suits a joke. The first establishes, the second develops, the third turns, and the fourth delivers, which maps onto the shape that comic writing generally uses, and the fixed division means the reader knows where the punchline falls before reaching it. Strips using three or six panels feel measurably different. Reading time is controlled by panel width. A wide panel takes longer to cross than a narrow one, so a cartoonist slows the reader before a reversal by widening the preceding panel, and this technique operates on readers who never notice it. Vertical formats change the rhythm entirely. The characters must be recognisable at very small size. Newspaper reproduction was coarse and the printed strip was often two inches high, so figures are built from a few strong shapes, faces are simplified to what survives reduction, and a cartoonist's style is shaped by the printing process as much as by preference. Continuity across decades is a distinct problem. A strip running for forty years must remain accessible to a reader encountering it today while rewarding one who has followed it since the beginning, and the solutions — characters who do not age, situations that reset, running references that need no explanation — define the form as much as the panel count does.

subject: 영화 포스터의 문법
title: Selling a film in one image
content: A film poster must work at a distance, in a moment, among competitors, and it must communicate genre, tone, and scale before anybody reads a word. The conventions that developed are consistent enough that audiences read them without instruction and notice immediately when one is broken. Genre is signalled by composition and colour before anything else. A single figure against a dark ground with cool light reads as one kind of film; a group arranged in a triangle under warm light reads as another; and audiences classify a poster correctly within a fraction of a second. Studios test this and the conventions are enforced commercially rather than artistically. The arrangement of faces encodes billing. Contracts specify whose name appears first, whose face is largest, and where each sits, so a poster is partly a legal document, and disputes over placement have delayed campaigns. Viewers read the hierarchy without knowing it was negotiated. Text carries information in a fixed order. Title, then a line of copy, then the credit block in a compressed typeface at the bottom, which almost nobody reads and which is contractually required, so the design must accommodate a block of unreadable type as a permanent element. Designers describe working around it. The best examples ignore most of this. Posters that became famous frequently reduce to a single graphic idea with no faces at all, which requires a studio confident enough to sell a film without showing its stars, and the rarity of such campaigns is a commercial fact rather than a failure of imagination among designers.

subject: 타이틀 시퀀스라는 형식
title: The short film before the film
content: Opening credits were originally a list. Somebody had to be named, so names appeared over a static card, and the sequence occupied a minute that nobody regarded as material. Treating that minute as a work in its own right produced a form with its own designers, its own history, and occasionally its own audiences. The shift is usually dated to the mid twentieth century, when designers began setting credits over animated graphics, over abstract movement, or over footage that established a mood without belonging to the story. The change was resisted by studios and adopted quickly once its effect was demonstrated, since a well made sequence prepares an audience in a way that the first scene cannot. The form has specific requirements. It must accommodate a fixed list of names in a required order, it must not exhaust its idea before the list ends, and it must arrive at the film's opening rather than at its own conclusion. Designers describe the last as the hardest, since a sequence that peaks too early leaves a gap. Music carries much of it. The sequence is frequently the only place where a score plays uninterrupted at length, so composers write for it as a piece, and several film themes are known primarily from these opening minutes. The relationship between the visual rhythm and the music is composed rather than fitted afterwards. Television adopted the form and then abandoned it. Series titles became elaborate, then shortened as viewers gained the ability to skip, and several recent productions place credits over the first scene instead — which returns the practice to where it began, for entirely different reasons.
